title: Contracts + Ownership
story: Contracts guarantee your logic is correct. Ownership guarantees your memory is safe. Together, they form the ultimate safety net — no crashes, no corruption, no surprises.
why: Combining contracts with ownership creates functions that are both logically correct AND memory safe — two layers of compiler-enforced protection.
analogy: Contracts are the rules of the road (don't speed, stop at red lights). Ownership is the seatbelt and airbags. Both keep you safe, but in different ways.
try_it: Add `ensures: from.balance >= 0.0` and `ensures: to.balance >= 0.0` to the transfer function. Then try to transfer more than the sender has.
tips: Use requires to validate business logic, &mut to ensure exclusive access
Contracts prevent logic errors; ownership prevents memory errors
A function with full contracts + correct ownership is provably safe
Write contracts BEFORE the body — they guide correct implementation
common_mistakes: Writing requires that duplicate what the type system already guarantees
Using owned parameters when &mut is sufficient — don't consume unnecessarily
Forgetting that &mut excludes other borrows — can't transfer between same account
